title: Order of Operations, Brackets and Laws of Arithmetic
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Number
summary: Use the order of operations, brackets and the commutative, associative and distributive laws to calculate accurately and simplify calculations.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Use the laws of arithmetic (the order you add or multiply does not matter; you can group numbers in a helpful way; you can split a number to multiply) and the order of operations to make calculations simpler (6Ni.02)
Understand that brackets can change the order in which you do the operations (6Ni.03)

blocks.text: Is 2 + 3 × 4 equal to 20 or 14? Everyone in the world must get the same answer, so mathematicians agree on an **order of operations**. On this page you will learn that order, how **brackets** change it, and three **laws of arithmetic** that let you do hard-looking calculations in your head.
Key words

items: operation
عملية — +, −, × or ÷
order of operations
ترتيب العمليات — the agreed order for working out a calculation
brackets ( )
الأقواس — work out the inside first
commutative law
خاصية الإبدال — you can swap the order: 3 + 8 = 8 + 3, 4 × 9 = 9 × 4
associative law
خاصية الدمج (التجميع) — you can group in any way: (5 + 7) + 3 = 5 + (7 + 3)
distributive law
خاصية التوزيع — split a number to multiply: 6 × 27 = 6 × 20 + 6 × 7
simplify
تبسيط — make a calculation easier to do
inverse

blocks.text: 1. The order of operations

items: **Brackets first.** Work out anything inside ( ).
**Then × and ÷**, working from left to right. Neither one comes before the other — whichever is further left is done first.
**Then + and −**, also from left to right.

blocks.title: BIDMAS / BODMAS
blocks.text: Some books use the word BIDMAS (Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction) to remember the order. The word puts D before M and A before S, but that is only to make it easy to say: × and ÷ have the **same** rank, and so do + and −. Always go left to right inside each rank. Indices are powers such as 4^{2}: if one appears, work it out straight after the brackets.

blocks.title: ترتيب العمليات
items: الأول: الأقواس ( ).
بعدين: الضرب والقسمة — بالترتيب من الشمال لليمين (مش الضرب الأول دايمًا).
في الآخر: الجمع والطرح — برضه من الشمال لليمين.

blocks.text: 2. Brackets change the order
Brackets tell you: **do this part first**, even if it is an addition or subtraction. The same numbers and signs can give different answers when the brackets move.

**Brackets in word problems.** "A family of 4 each buy a cinema ticket for E£45 and popcorn for E£15." Each person spends 45 + 15, so the total is **4 × (45 + 15)** = 4 × 60 = **E£240**. Without brackets, 4 × 45 + 15 = 195 would only pay for one popcorn.

**Brackets that do not change anything.** In 3 + (4 × 5) the brackets are not needed, because × is done first anyway. Brackets around a multiplication or division in a sum do not change the answer — but they can make it clearer.
3. The laws of arithmetic
These laws are not new rules to learn by heart — they describe what you already know about numbers. They help you choose an **easier order** to calculate.
Commutative law: swap the order
For **addition and multiplication**, the order does not matter: 3 + 8 = 8 + 3 and 3 × 5 = 5 × 3.

blocks.text: It does **not** work for subtraction or division: 10 − 4 = 6 but 4 − 10 = −6; 12 ÷ 3 = 4 but 3 ÷ 12 = ¼.
Associative law: group in a helpful way

When you add or multiply three or more numbers, you can choose which pair to do first: (17 + 26) + 4 = 17 + (26 + 4) = 17 + 30 = **47**. (25 × 7) × 4 = 7 × (25 × 4) = 7 × 100 = **700**. Look for pairs that make 10, 100, 1000 (like 25 × 4, 5 × 20, 38 + 62).
Distributive law: split a number
To multiply a number by a sum, multiply each part and add: 6 × 27 = 6 × (20 + 7) = 6 × 20 + 6 × 7 = 120 + 42 = **162**. The area model shows why.

blocks.text: It works with subtraction too, which is great for numbers just below a tens number: 8 × 19 = 8 × (20 − 1) = 160 − 8 = **152**.

blocks.text: Division can be split in the same way, as long as you split the number being divided: 96 ÷ 4 = 80 ÷ 4 + 16 ÷ 4 = 20 + 4 = **24**.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Work out 18 − 3 × 4. [1 mark]

items: No brackets. Look for × or ÷: 3 × 4 = 12.
Then subtract: 18 − 12 = 6.
**Answer: 6**

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** 18 − 3 = 15, then 15 × 4 = 60. Multiplication must come before subtraction.
**Worked example 2** — (a) Work out 40 ÷ (2 + 6). (b) Work out 40 ÷ 2 + 6. [2 marks]

items: (a) Brackets first: 2 + 6 = 8. Then 40 ÷ 8 = **5**.
(b) No brackets, so divide first: 40 ÷ 2 = 20. Then 20 + 6 = **26**.
The brackets changed the answer from 26 to 5.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Work out 7 + 24 ÷ 6 − 2 × 3. [1 mark]

items: Do every × and ÷ first: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 2 × 3 = 6.
Rewrite: 7 + 4 − 6.
Left to right: 7 + 4 = 11, 11 − 6 = 5.
**Answer: 5**

blocks.text: **Tip:** underline each × and ÷ part first, then rewrite the line. This stops you losing track.
**Worked example 4** — Put brackets in this calculation to make it correct: 5 + 3 × 6 − 2 = 32 [1 mark]

items: Without brackets: 5 + 18 − 2 = 21. Too small, so we need to add or subtract before multiplying.

blocks.text: **Technique:** think about which two numbers multiply to give the target: 32 = 8 × 4, and 8 = 5 + 3, 4 = 6 − 2.
**Worked example 5** — Use the laws of arithmetic to work out these mentally. Show how. (a) 4 × 37 × 25 (b) 8 × 49 [2 marks]

items: (a) Change the order and group: (4 × 25) × 37 = 100 × 37 = **3700**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Mona buys 3 notebooks at E£28 each and pays with a E£100 note. Write one calculation for her change, then work it out. [2 marks]

items: Cost of notebooks: 3 × 28. Change = 100 minus the cost.
One calculation: **100 − 3 × 28** (the brackets 100 − (3 × 28) are allowed but not needed).

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** writing (100 − 3) × 28 — that would be 2716!

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Working strictly from left to right through the whole line: 2 + 3 × 4 is 14, not 20.
Always doing × before ÷ (or + before −). They are equal partners — go left to right: 24 ÷ 4 × 2 = 12; 20 − 8 + 3 = 15.
Forgetting to finish inside the brackets first: in (6 + 2 × 3) do 2 × 3 before the + — the answer inside is 12.
Using the commutative law for subtraction or division: 4 − 10 is not the same as 10 − 4.
Splitting with the distributive law but multiplying only one part: 6 × 27 is not 6 × 20 + 7.
Writing a word problem without brackets when you need them: 4 × 45 + 15 ≠ 4 × (45 + 15).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Work out" a calculation with mixed operations — usually on Paper 1 (no calculator).
"Put brackets in to make the calculation correct" or "Draw a ring around the calculation that has the answer 30".
"Write the missing number" in a distributive split: 6 × 47 = 6 × 40 + 6 × ☐.
"Tick the calculations that give the same answer as 8 × 46" — use the laws, not long multiplication.
"Explain the mistake" — say which operation should be done first and give the correct answer.
Technique: after you finish, check by putting your answer back — and on Paper 2, a calculator also uses the order of operations, so type the whole line in (with brackets) to check.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Order of operations practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, no calculator. Underline the part you will do first in each one. Full working appears when you check.

questions.e: × and ÷ first, left to right: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12. Then 6 + 12 = 18.

questions.q: Where should the brackets go to make this correct?  4 × 5 + 3 = 32
questions.e: 4 × (5 + 3) = 4 × 8 = 32. Without brackets (or with brackets round 4 × 5) the answer is 20 + 3 = 23.

questions.q: Use the laws of arithmetic to work out 25 × 9 × 4 without writing a long calculation.
Which statement is NOT always true for all numbers a, b and c?
questions.e: Subtraction is not commutative: 10 − 4 = 6 but 4 − 10 = −6. The other three are the commutative and associative laws.

questions.q: Which calculation gives the same answer as 8 × 46?
questions.e: Distributive law: 46 = 40 + 6, so 8 × 46 = 8 × 40 + 8 × 6 = 320 + 48 = 368. The others give 326, 248 and 1920.

questions.q: A shop has 5 boxes of 12 pens and 8 loose pens. Write one calculation for the total number of pens, then work it out.
questions.e: 5 × 12 + 8 = 60 + 8 = 68 pens. (Multiplication is done first, so no brackets are needed.)

questions.q: Nadia works out 12 − 6 − 2 like this: "6 − 2 = 4, then 12 − 4 = 8." Explain her mistake and write the correct answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explains that subtractions must be done from left to right (12 − 6 first) AND gives the correct answer 4. Accept: "she worked out 12 − (6 − 2)" with answer 4. Do not accept the answer 4 with no explanation.
questions.e: + and − are done from left to right: 12 − 6 = 6, then 6 − 2 = 4. Nadia worked it out as if it were 12 − (6 − 2) = 8. The correct answer is 4.

questions.q: Put one or two pairs of brackets into this calculation to make it correct:  3 + 5 × 4 − 1 = 24
questions.ms: 1 mark: (3 + 5) × (4 − 1) = 24. Accept extra brackets that do not change the value, e.g. ((3 + 5) × (4 − 1)). Do not accept (3 + 5) × 4 − 1 (= 31) or 3 + 5 × (4 − 1) (= 18).

questions.e: Brackets first, and inside the brackets × before +: 2 × 9 = 18, 6 + 18 = 24 (M1). Then ÷ before −: 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Finally 48 − 8 = 40 (A1).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Order: Brackets → × and ÷ (left to right) → + and − (left to right).
Brackets change the order: 2 + 3 × 4 = 14 but (2 + 3) × 4 = 20.
Commutative: you can swap the order for + and × (never for − or ÷).
Associative: group numbers to make 10, 100 or 1000 first: 25 × 7 × 4 = 100 × 7.
Distributive: split a number to multiply: 6 × 27 = 6 × 20 + 6 × 7; 8 × 19 = 8 × 20 − 8.
